name: Urea cream

card.summary: Urea cream is a moisturiser that hydrates and softens rough, dry skin, and is used to smooth texture and ease irritation from other skincare actives.
card.note: Can sting on broken or irritated skin; higher concentrations are more keratolytic.

quick.overview:
Urea cream is a moisturiser containing urea, a compound that attracts water into the skin and, at higher concentrations, loosens thick or rough skin. It is used on dry, rough or bumpy skin to leave it smoother and softer.

A 2021 randomised trial compared creams with different urea concentrations for plantar skin hydration, and a 2024 clinical trial evaluated a 20% urea cream for keratosis pilaris. In looksmaxxing forums it appears as a recovery step alongside retinoids and microneedling.
quick.how: People apply it like any moisturiser to dry areas such as the body, hands or feet, and some use it on the face on nights between active products. One forum user describes alternating a tretinoin night with a urea cream night plus occasional derma stamping. Strength varies by product, with lower percentages used for general hydration and higher ones for rough patches.
quick.risks: Urea can irritate skin, eyes and the respiratory tract, according to Wikipedia, and may sting on cracked or inflamed skin. Higher concentrations are intended for thick, rough skin and can be too strong for sensitive facial skin.

lead: Urea cream is a topical moisturiser that contains urea, a small molecule that is also a natural component of the skin's own moisturising factor. In looks terms it is used to make dry, rough or flaky skin feel and look softer and smoother, to treat the rough bumps of keratosis pilaris on the arms and thighs, to soften calluses and cracked heels, and to cushion the skin between stronger actives such as retinoids.[1][2][10]

A 2018 review in Dermatologic Therapy summarised the clinical literature on topical urea and described a split by strength: formulations at or below 10% urea act mainly as moisturisers, while those above 10% are keratolytic, meaning they loosen and shed the thick outer layer of dead skin cells.[2] Wikipedia lists 40% preparations among the products used for conditions such as psoriasis, xerosis, ichthyosis, keratosis, calluses and, under an occlusive dressing, nonsurgical removal of diseased nails.[1]

Randomised and open-label trials have examined urea creams on foot-skin hydration, keratosis pilaris and the darkened, thickened skin of acanthosis nigricans, and a 2024 systematic review graded urea cream among the topical options for acanthosis nigricans.[3][4][5][6] On looksmax.org the product appears as a recovery moisturiser that users alternate with tretinoin nights and derma-stamping.[7]

angle.text: Urea cream hydrates skin and, at higher strengths, loosens rough scale so skin looks smoother and feels softer. People use it on the body for keratosis pilaris and dry patches, on hands and feet, and as a buffer between irritating actives such as tretinoin.

paras: Cosmetic and medical use overlap closely for urea creams. The most common appearance goals are softer, less flaky skin on the body, hands and feet; a smoother surface where keratosis pilaris causes rough, goose-bump-like papules; and softening of calluses and heels.[1][2]

Wikipedia's article on keratosis pilaris lists urea alongside lactic, glycolic and salicylic acid among moisturising or keratolytic agents used in topical treatment, and notes that improvement often takes months and the bumps are likely to return.[8]

Urea is highly water-soluble, and Wikipedia notes that urea-containing creams promote rehydration of the skin.[1] The Dermatologic Therapy review describes urea as part of the skin's natural moisturising factor and links its use to conditions where the skin barrier is compromised, such as xerosis, atopic dermatitis and psoriasis.[2]

Keratosis pilaris is a common condition of rough follicular bumps, and urea is one of the standard keratolytic moisturisers named for it.[8] A 2024 open-label study tested a 20% urea cream on keratosis pilaris (see Clinical studies).[5]

Acanthosis nigricans presents as dark, velvety patches in skin folds such as the neck and armpits. A 2024 systematic review of 19 trials graded topical tretinoin highest and endorsed adapalene gel, urea cream and fractional carbon dioxide laser at the next grade.[4] A 2022 trial compared two urea strengths on the neck in adolescents.[6]

Wikipedia states that 40% urea under an occlusive dressing can be used for nonsurgical debridement of diseased or dystrophic nails, and a Japanese review lists urea cream under occlusion among the chemical nail-removal approaches used for onychomycosis.[1][9]

Urea binds water through extensive hydrogen bonding, which is why it is a humectant that holds moisture in the outer skin layer.[1][2] At higher concentrations it disrupts the intercellular matrix that holds dead skin cells together, which is the basis of its keratolytic effect on thickened skin and nails.[1][2]
The 2018 review also reports that urea can increase the penetration of anti-inflammatory and antifungal drugs applied with it.[2]

Urea was first obtained from evaporated urine in the early 1700s, was named by Fourcroy and Vauquelin in 1799, and was synthesised from inorganic starting materials by Friedrich Wöhler in 1828, an episode often cited in the history of organic chemistry.[1] Its dermatological use as a cream was already being discussed in the podiatry literature in 1971, in a Journal of the American Podiatry Association article titled 'Urea cream for dry skin'.[10]

Urea cream appears on looksmax.org as a recovery product. In one thread, a user says daily tretinoin left his skin red and peeling, so he moved to every other night and does a derma stamp periodically; a reply recommends alternating tretinoin with urea cream and a weekly derma stamp for two months, and another reply says the combination will 'de-age' skin.[7]
The forum thread is anecdotal and describes one person's routine rather than a study; no published trial has tested urea cream combined with tretinoin and microneedling.

Wikipedia states that urea can irritate the skin, eyes and respiratory tract; it also describes urea as practically non-toxic by mouth based on animal data, and says repeated prolonged contact with fertiliser-form urea may cause dermatitis.[1] In the 2022 acanthosis nigricans trial both strengths were reported as well tolerated without serious local reactions, and in the 2024 keratosis pilaris study no significant adverse events were reported.[5][6]
The 2018 review frames strength as the main variable, with lower percentages acting as moisturisers and higher ones as keratolytics.[2]

A 2021 randomised trial in the Journal of Tissue Viability assigned 60 adults aged 20 to 35 to placebo, 5% urea or 20% urea cream on the feet and measured hydration with a Corneometer; the 20% cream differed significantly from placebo at all measured sites, while 5% did not consistently differ from placebo.[3]

A 2024 open-label, 4-week, noncomparative study of a 20% urea cream applied once daily in 30 adults with keratosis pilaris reported significant improvement in smoothness and texture at 1 and 4 weeks, high participant satisfaction with how their skin felt, and no significant adverse events.[5]

A 2022 randomised double-blind trial in 40 adolescents with neck acanthosis nigricans compared 20% and 10% urea creams over 8 weeks. Spectrophotometer-measured hyperpigmentation improved by about 22.5% with 20% urea and 10.7% with 10% urea (p = 0.001), and both strengths were well tolerated.[6]

Urea cream has also been studied as a preventive for hand-foot syndrome, a chemotherapy side effect. A 2025 randomised trial of 216 patients receiving capecitabine found any-grade hand-foot syndrome in 56% of the urea group and 62.4% of the usual-care group, a difference that was not statistically significant, and a 2026 network meta-analysis of 13 trials found topical diclofenac and celecoxib significantly reduced moderate-to-severe cases.[11][12] These oncology studies concern a medical condition rather than cosmetic use.

timeline.event: Herman Boerhaave obtains urea from evaporated urine, one of several early isolations credited to different chemists.[1]
Fourcroy and Vauquelin coin the name 'urea' for the crystals first obtained by Rouelle.[1]
Friedrich Wöhler synthesises urea from inorganic starting materials.[1]
The Journal of the American Podiatry Association carries an article on urea cream for dry skin.[10]
A review in Dermatologic Therapy summarises clinical evidence on topical urea and its concentration-dependent moisturising and keratolytic roles.[2]
Randomised trial compares placebo, 5% and 20% urea creams on foot-skin hydration.[3]
Randomised trial compares 20% and 10% urea creams for acanthosis nigricans in adolescents.[6]
Open-label study of a 20% urea cream for keratosis pilaris; a systematic review grades urea cream among acanthosis nigricans topicals.[4][5]

lore.intro: Urea cream is a minor topic in looksmaxxing forums, where it is mentioned as a gentle moisturiser used between retinoid nights and microneedling.[7]

claims.claim: Alternating tretinoin and urea cream with derma stamping will 'de-age' skin
claims.believers: A forum reply says the combination will de-age skin, and the original poster, who moved tretinoin to alternate nights after redness and peeling, adds a periodic derma stamp.[7]
claims.experts: Trials of urea creams have measured hydration, keratosis pilaris smoothness and neck pigmentation; none has tested this combination.[3][5][6]

claims.claim: Urea cream calms the irritation and dryness that retinoids cause
claims.believers: Users treat the urea night as a recovery night between tretinoin applications.[7]
claims.experts: The 2018 review describes urea as a component of natural moisturising factor that supports hydration and barrier function, but it does not address retinoid irritation specifically.[2]

claims.claim: Higher-percentage urea smooths rough, bumpy skin better than low-percentage urea
claims.believers: Users and product descriptions pair lower strengths with general hydration and higher ones with rough patches.
claims.experts: The 2018 review describes a keratolytic effect above 10%; the foot-hydration trial found 20% differed from placebo at all sites while 5% did not, and the acanthosis nigricans trial found 20% outperformed 10%.[2][3][6]

claims.believers: Users on skincare forums report smoother arms after consistent use.[8]
claims.experts: A 20% urea cream improved smoothness over 4 weeks in a 30-person open-label study; Wikipedia notes that improvement often takes months and the bumps tend to return.[5][8]
